analysis.one_liner: Lets regulators claw back bonuses and stock profits of executives at failed big banks.
analysis.headline: The bill was written, reported by the Senate Banking Committee, and placed on the Senate calendar for 18 months, but drew zero cosponsors and never got a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2023 bank failures, this bill would let federal regulators take back up to two years of bonuses, stock-sale profits, severance, and golden parachute pay from senior executives who ran a bank into failure, and would let regulators remove executives for gross negligence. It would also raise the cap on civil penalties for senior executives from $1 million to $3 million, hold them liable for reckless as well as knowing violations, require public reports after a big bank fails, and tighten rules on who can buy a failed bank. It applied only to banks with more than $10 billion in assets; smaller banks were exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Depositors, the FDIC's deposit insurance fund, and ultimately taxpayers, because money clawed back from failed-bank executives goes back into the receivership estate instead of leaving with the executives. Bank employees and communities also benefit from executives with stronger incentives to keep banks sound.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Depositors, the FDIC fund, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: If a bank with over $10 billion in assets fails, regulators could recover bonuses, incentive and equity compensation, severance, golden parachute benefits, and stock-sale profits from the previous 24 months from any senior executive responsible for the failure [S2][S4].

Regulators could remove a senior executive at a bank of any size for gross negligence, breach of fiduciary duty, or failing to carry out responsibilities for governance, operations, or risk and financial management [S2][S4].

The cap on the highest tier of civil money penalties for senior executives would rise from $1 million to $3 million, and executives could be penalized for reckless violations, not just knowing ones [S4].

Regulators would have to publish a public report on the management, supervision, and regulation of any failed bank over $10 billion within 180 days, the Federal Reserve would report publicly every six months on its supervision, and the regulator's inspector general would report to Congress on what caused the failure [S4].
Regulators could approve a large bank's acquisition of a failed bank only when no other qualifying buyer had applied, limiting rescue sales that hand failed banks to favored acquirers [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Senior executives at banks over $10 billion in assets, who would face clawback exposure, easier removal, and higher penalties; and large banks generally, which would face governance and accountability standards and tighter rules on acquiring failed banks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives and boards of big banks

drawbacks.text: Banking groups argued that clawing back compensation and raising penalties could make it harder to recruit and retain experienced bank executives, and the bill itself includes a Sense of Congress that it should not be used to penalize executives of healthy, well-managed institutions [S4].

Clawbacks apply only to executives deemed responsible for the failure and exempt executives with less than 18 months on the job, so executives could dispute responsibility and some accountable leaders could escape recovery [S4].
Tighter conditions on selling failing banks could, in a fast-moving crisis, complicate the quick sale the FDIC sometimes needs to keep deposits and jobs intact [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real but backloaded: it changes incentives before a crisis and recovers money after one, instead of leaving the deposit insurance fund to absorb losses while failed executives keep their bonuses. The costs are mostly compliance burden on large banks and a harder recruiting pitch for big-bank leadership. The bill was carefully scoped — a $10 billion threshold, a responsible-executive limit, and an 18-month exemption — which limits collateral damage to well-run banks. On balance the benefits to depositors and the insurance fund outweigh the costs, though the bill would not prevent failures on its own; it changes who pays for them.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee reported the bill to the Senate floor and it sat on the Senate calendar for a year and a half, but no floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Chairman Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on June 22, 2023 and reported it to the Senate the same day as a committee original measure, without a written report, placing it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 115 [S1][S6].
No senator joined as a cosponsor; the bill finished with zero [S5].
The Banking Committee held hearings on the bill in December 2023, March 2024, and May 2024, but the Senate never took it up for a vote [S6].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still on the calendar, so the clawback authority, higher penalties, and reporting requirements never became law [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senior executives of large banks are better off: they face no new clawback exposure, removal authority, or higher penalty cap, and the deposit insurance fund continues to absorb the cost of executive failures.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big-bank executives and the banking industry

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and reported it to the Senate as a committee original measure, placing it on the Senate calendar.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote during the 18 months it sat on the calendar.

against.name: Banking industry groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly criticized executive clawback and accountability proposals as making it harder to recruit and retain bank leadership.

sides.party_line_note: No senator of either party cosponsored the bill and no roll call was ever taken, so the partisan split was never measured [S5].

industries.industry: Executives of large banks (over $10 billion in assets)
industries.note: They would face clawback of two years of bonuses, equity compensation, severance, and golden parachute pay if their bank failed on their watch, plus removal authority and a higher, recklessness-based penalty standard. Their interest in keeping that compensation runs against depositors and the insurance fund that cover failure losses.

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill imposes governance and accountability standards and limits their ability to acquire failed banks when other qualified buyers exist. Compliance costs are modest, but the merger limits reduce a rescue-sales advantage.
They are explicitly exempt from the governance standards and clawback requirements, so they avoid the compliance burden that would fall on large competitors.
